steps.title: 1. Problem analysis and identification of relevant topics
steps.description:
We are asked to evaluate a definite integral of the form ∫₀^{π/8} x·sin(2x) dx.

Key observations:
• The integrand is a product of x (an algebraic function) and sin(2x) (a trigonometric function).
• For products of a polynomial (or linear) factor and a trigonometric factor, the standard antidifferentiation technique is Integration by Parts.

Curriculum links:
• “INTEGRATION—CONTINUED: find integrals using integration by parts.”
• We will also use basic differentiation (FUNCTIONS AND DIFFERENTIATION) to obtain du and v during the procedure.
steps.hints: Recall the Integration-by-Parts formula: ∫ u dv = u·v − ∫ v du.

steps.title: 2. Choose the parts for Integration by Parts
steps.description:
Let u = x (because its derivative simplifies) and dv = sin(2x) dx (which is easy to integrate).
Then: du = dx,  v = ∫ sin(2x) dx = −cos(2x)/2
steps.hints: Pick u so that differentiating it simplifies the expression; pick dv so that you can integrate it easily.

steps.title: 3. Apply the Integration‐by‐Parts formula
steps.description:
∫ x·sin(2x) dx = u·v − ∫ v·du
= x·(−cos(2x)/2) − ∫ (−cos(2x)/2)·dx
= −(x cos(2x))/2 + (1/2)∫ cos(2x) dx
steps.hints: Be careful with the minus signs produced by integrating sin(2x).

steps.title: 4. Integrate the remaining cosine term
steps.description:
∫ cos(2x) dx = sin(2x)/2 (because derivative of sin(2x) is 2 cos(2x)).
Therefore the antiderivative becomes
F(x) = −(x cos(2x))/2 + (1/2)·(sin(2x)/2)
= −(x cos(2x))/2 + sin(2x)/4
steps.hints: Check by differentiating F(x) to make sure you recover x sin(2x).

steps.title: 5. Evaluate the antiderivative at the limits 0 and π/8
6. Numerical simplification
steps.hints: Factor out √2/32 to combine the two terms neatly.
